It seems like someone else reverted the edit. This is a borderline case, but I do feel like the edit is justified for the grammar consistency and the in-universe containment explanation.

(That said… it looks like you've reversed the quotes. The second quote is the current version, and the one before that is your proposed change.)

item.title: Edit justification
item.content:encoded:
Simple verb tense change,

SCP-124 is to be kept in a 4.2 m x 2.1 m stone pit in its containment cell. The pit is to be 1.5 metres deep.

to

SCP-124 is to be kept in a 4.2 m x 2.1 m stone pit in its containment cell. The pit is 1.5 metres deep.

reason 1- Grammatically, verb tenses should conform sentences to sentences nearby, so as to convey coherent information.
reason 2- Because "is to be" implies that the containment procedures can be reproduced elsewhere in case of containment breach.

Also, justifying simply because of insecurities created from past mistakes.

item.content:encoded:
So the plot grows humans or scary animals into monsters, but a puppy grows into a nice dog instead of, for example, some kind of wolf thing? And plants just grow normally, but faster? Seems inconsistent to me.

Containment should be updated to keep the soil behind a sealed door, with the chamber constantly disinfected. Super-diseases will grow otherwise. The fact that the soil was previously contained exposed in Detroit makes one wonder how this didn't happen already. And from there I have to question how the plot came to the Foundation's attention… kids growing marijuana shouldn't register. Authorities having to clear away a two-story-tall pot plant might. The link between the outside world and the Foundation's attention needs to be firmed up.

Also nit-picky, but there's no need to list both the area and volume of the soil. 14 m3 will make any area you want, depending on the depth and shape you choose.

item.title: Locked box test
item.content:encoded:
Whether it passes the locked box test for Safe hinges on whether you should account for a bug crawling into the box through the keyhole, and whether the plot of soil is genuinely obtainable to lock away.

However containers which seal off outside matter are almost trivial to make in modern day. Such technology was available to Francesco Redi and Louis Pasteur in 1668 and 1859 respectively, which they used to such a degree of success they were great contributions to disproving spontaneous generation.

That considered, so long as the soil can actually be extracted from the rest of the earth and locked away, I'm of the belief it should be classified Safe.
